case_study_insert.main_stem: Ridgeway Aggregates (RGA) is a private limited company in the quarrying and crushed-rock aggregates sector, employing a workforce of 62. Founded in 2005 by Duncan Ridgeway, it supplies graded aggregate to regional construction firms and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership on safety-critical sites. RGA plans to invest $720,000 in a new mobile crushing and screening plant with dust-suppression and water-recycling technology, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $20.00, and currently produces 60,000 units a year. RGA faces two problems: quality complaints about off-spec grading have risen to 4.2% of loads, and site absenteeism has reached 8%. Duncan wants growth without risking its extraction licence.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The quarry dispatched 15,000 tonnes last quarter at an off-spec rejection rate of 4.2%, up from 2.6% a year earlier. Customer quality complaints rose from 12 to 27 per month, and average delivery turnaround is 4.1 days. Diesel use per tonne fell 3.0% after a trial of the dust-suppression system, while dust complaints from nearby residents numbered 9. A survey of 300 regional contractors found that 58% would switch supplier for reliably graded, lower-dust aggregate and 47% check a quarry's environmental record before tendering. A skills audit shows 18 of 62 staff lack certification on the new screening plant; accredited external courses cost $780 per operator.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Ridgeway Aggregates for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans such as RGA's $450,000 expansion loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $12.80 to $13.55 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills across quarrying and haulage. (3) Diesel and tyre input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year, while construction output grew 2.8% and regional demand for graded aggregate increased 3.1%.

questions.question_text: RGA plans to fund part of its $720,000 crushing-plant expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for RGA of using $270,000 retained profit to fund the expansion instead of taking a larger bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit is internally generated, so using the $270,000 avoids interest and capital repayments on a larger loan and leaves RGA's cash flow intact at a time when it already services a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and carries fixed costs of $360,000 a year. Every dollar of interest saved can be spent on the dust-suppression and water-recycling plant without raising the $20.00 selling price for construction clients, which matters when 58% of surveyed contractors say they would switch supplier for more reliable, lower-dust aggregate.

Point 2: Funding from retained profit keeps decision-making with Duncan Ridgeway and the existing owners, since no lender can attach covenants to how the $720,000 mobile crushing plant is operated. It also avoids the repossession risk that a bigger loan would create if the 4.2% off-spec rejection rate persisted and cash generation disappointed. Retained profit is therefore the lower-risk source for a quarrying business whose hierarchical, safety-critical sites already work within tight margins.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over a larger loan (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to RGA, its $720,000 expansion, existing $450,000 loan and contractor survey evidence.

questions.question_text: RGA is launching its new dust-suppressed, lower-dust graded aggregate to regional contractors. Consider national trade-press advertising, local radio sponsorship, or direct sales visits to construction firms. Which should RGA choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National trade-press advertising: A campaign in construction and quarrying journals would build awareness of RGA's new dust-suppressed aggregate among the 300 contractors surveyed, many of whom specify materials on regional projects. It reaches a professional audience and supports a premium positioning. However, print advertising is costly for a 62-employee firm already funding a $720,000 plant, and much of the readership lies outside RGA's regional delivery radius, so spend would be wasted where the quarry cannot physically supply.

Local radio sponsorship: Sponsoring regional radio is cheaper and repeats the message to local contract managers and hauliers who actually buy RGA's output. It suits a time-sensitive launch and reinforces the lower-dust story. Its weakness is reach and detail: radio cannot demonstrate graded consistency or the 3.0% diesel reduction, and it will not persuade the 47% of contractors who check environmental records before tendering.

Direct sales visits: RGA's technical team can call on the largest regional contractors, present test certificates and a credible plan to bring the 4.2% off-spec rate back towards the 2.6% level of a year ago, and quote for tailored grading. This uses the existing sales force, gives immediate feedback and targets the 58% who would switch for reliability. It is slower to scale and depends on staff time where absenteeism is 8%.

Recommendation: RGA should choose direct sales visits, supported by short trade-press notices. Direct visits target exactly the regional contractors who buy and specify aggregate, let RGA prove the lower-dust, better-graded product and win the 58% willing to switch, at a cost far below national press. National advertising is rejected as unaffordable and geographically wasteful; radio is rejected because it cannot carry the technical evidence that 47% of environmentally-checking buyers demand.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to RGA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of RGA with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Discusses all three options in the context of RGA and ends with a justified recommendation explaining why trade-press advertising and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: RGA's off-spec rejection rate has risen to 4.2% and site absenteeism has reached 8%. Explain two benefits for RGA of using its hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership to address these problems.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A hierarchical structure gives RGA clear lines of authority and a short, well-understood chain of command on safety-critical crushing sites, so when the off-spec rejection rate reached 4.2% management can issue one unambiguous grading standard and know it will be followed. Autocratic leadership lets Duncan Ridgeway act quickly to stop non-conforming loads leaving the quarry, protecting the construction-client relationships that underpin 60,000 units of annual output and the $20.00 selling price.

Point 2: The same clarity helps tackle 8% site absenteeism. With defined roles and autocratic decisions, supervisors can reallocate shifts immediately when crushers are short-staffed, keeping the $720,000 crushing plant running and limiting disruption to customers. Formal downward communication also makes safety and quality expectations explicit, reducing the chance that rushed work raises defects further. In a quarrying firm with 62 staff and fixed costs of $360,000 a year, this top-down control protects both output and the extraction licence that the business depends on.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of hierarchical/autocratic structures (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to RGA's 4.2% defects, 8% absenteeism, output and expansion.

questions.question_text: RGA must train 18 operators on the new screening plant. Consider accredited external courses at $780 per operator or on-the-job coaching on the line. Which should RGA choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Accredited external courses at $780 per operator: Sending the 18 uncertified staff to an accredited provider gives a recognised qualification, up-to-date screening techniques and an external check on competence, which matters when 4.2% of loads are off-spec and clients are complaining. For 18 staff the direct fee is $780 x 18 = $14,040, affordable against the $720,000 investment. The drawbacks are cost, lost production while operators are away, and generic content that may not cover RGA's exact plant settings.

On-the-job coaching: Training at the screening line is machine-specific, costs no fees and keeps all 18 operators productive while they learn, so output of 60,000 units is protected. Senior operators can demonstrate the dust-suppression routine directly. However, trainers pass on their own bad habits, formal certification is weak, and with 8% absenteeism the sessions may be interrupted by staffing shortages.

Decision: RGA should choose accredited external courses for the 18 operators, followed by on-site coaching. The recognised certificate directly addresses the 4.2% off-spec problem and the 27 monthly complaints; $14,040 is small beside $720,000. On-the-job coaching alone is rejected because it cannot provide the formal evidence that contractors and the quarry's safety regulators require.

A further consideration is the wider effect on RGA's 62 staff: sending 18 operators away at $780 each will strain an already stretched workforce where absenteeism is 8%, so scheduling should avoid peak delivery weeks. If the accredited course raises grading accuracy and cuts the 4.2% off-spec rate, the reduction in rejected loads should recoup the $14,040 fee through protected revenue on 60,000 units.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to RGA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of RGA.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, certification and disruption, rejecting the alternative.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how RGA's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 45,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $8.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety against 60,000-unit output; pricing and discount modelling against $360,000 fixed costs; loan-service feasibility for the $720,000 plant; and unit-cost benchmarking at $18.00 to tackle waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs / Contribution per unit. Substitution: $360,000 / ($20.00 - $12.00) = $360,000 / $8.00 = 45,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 45,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price - Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $20.00 - $12.00 = $8.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $8.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways RGA's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 45,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 60,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 15,000 units, to judge whether the new $720,000 crushing plant is justified.
2. Contribution of $8.00 lets RGA model a discount to contractors: a $1.00 cut to $19.00 would leave $7.00 contribution, showing how much volume must rise to keep covering $360,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing the $8.00 contribution and $360,000 fixed costs helps set volume targets that service the $450,000 bank loan before further capital is committed.
4. Average total cost of $360,000 / 60,000 + $12.00 = $18.00 a unit can be benchmarked each quarter to detect waste and track off-spec rejection rates.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate RGA's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has RGA's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.5%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 20.0%
ROCE 2025 = 25.0%

Detailed workings: Gross profit of $1,600,000 on revenue of $4,000,000 gives 40.0% in 2024; $2,250,000 on $5,000,000 gives 45.0% in 2025. Operating profit of $500,000 on $4,000,000 revenue is 12.5%, and $750,000 on $5,000,000 is 15.0% in 2025. Returns on the capital base are $500,000 / $2,500,000 = 20.0% and $750,000 / $3,000,000 = 25.0%.

Evaluation: Every margin moved favourably. The gross margin rose from 40.0% to 45.0%, meaning a smaller share of revenue was absorbed by cost of sales even as revenue grew from $4,000,000 to $5,000,000. Operating margin improved from 12.5% to 15.0%, showing operating profit outpaced revenue, helped by tighter control after the complaints about off-spec grading. The return on capital climbed from 20.0% to 25.0%, so the extra $500,000 of capital employed is being used more effectively. The operating margin is the stronger evidence because it reflects RGA's underlying trading performance after operating costs, whereas the gross margin can move with input prices alone. Capital employed also grew, so the ROCE rise is driven by profit growth rather than a shrinking asset base. Interest payable rose only from $40,000 to $55,000, so financing costs are not the cause.

Conclusion: RGA's financial performance has clearly improved. All three measures moved in the same favourable direction and the improvement is broad-based rather than the result of a one-off cut in capital employed.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures with little or no accurate calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three profitability measures for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of margins and capital use and a justified conclusion, naming the stronger evidence.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for RGA of introducing water-recycling and dust-suppression technology at its crushing plant.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Water-recycling and dust-suppression technology directly addresses RGA's local environmental complaints, which numbered 9 last quarter, and builds on the 3.0% diesel-use reduction already trialled. It strengthens the lower-dust positioning that 58% of surveyed contractors value, protecting the $20.00 selling price and the 60,000-unit output from the new $720,000 crushing plant. Because 47% of buyers check environmental records before tendering, the technology helps RGA retain and win regional construction listings.

Disadvantage: The equipment raises fixed costs and may push the $12.00 variable cost per unit higher, squeezing the $8.00 contribution if the quarry cannot pass costs on to price-sensitive contractors. Water-recycling systems also need maintenance and skilled operators, and with 18 of 62 staff uncertified and absenteeism at 8%, a breakdown could halt the screening line and worsen the 4.2% off-spec rate. The financial return depends on environmental benefits that are difficult to monetise in the short term.

Duncan should compare this environmental benefit with the cost of the 4.2% rejection rate before approving further capital.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to RGA's survey data, complaint figures and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in diesel and tyre input costs will affect RGA. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): The increase is 0.75 percentage points. If RGA's $450,000 expansion loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.75% x $450,000 = $3,375 a year, a small sum beside $360,000 fixed costs. If the loan is fixed-rate, the immediate cash effect is nil. Higher rates could still make future borrowing dearer and may cool regional construction demand.

Minimum wage rise (5.9%, to $13.55 per hour): RGA employs a workforce of 62 in quarrying and haulage roles that are largely hourly-paid, so wage costs rise and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual wage bill can be invented; the honest test is productivity, where 60,000 units / 62 staff is about 968 units per worker. If output per worker holds, the rise is affordable; if 8% absenteeism erodes it, unit labour cost climbs and the $8.00 contribution narrows.

Input cost inflation (9.6% on diesel and tyres): The insert does not split the $12.00 variable cost, so only a bounded figure can be shown: if the whole variable cost rose by 9.6%, that adds 9.6% x $12.00 = $1.152, about $1.15 a unit; across 60,000 units that is $69,120 a year. Contribution would fall from $8.00 toward about $6.85.

Conclusion: The 9.6% input-cost rise has the greatest impact. It compounds on every unit sold, directly erodes the contribution that justifies the $720,000 plant and cannot be removed by fixing a loan rate. The interest rise is at most $3,375, and the wage rise can be offset by productivity; neither strikes every unit.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to RGA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on RGA's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes with shown derivations from insert figures and a justified greatest-impact judgement rejecting the other two.
